source: NASA SPHEREx DR1 Level 2 spectral images via IRSA (irsa.ipac.caltech.edu)

target.name: RW Aurigae
target.note: A young binary T Tauri star that dims by magnitudes for months at a time when its tidally disrupted disc passes in front of it. Brightness, not position, is the story.
target.look_for: This one does not move — it blinks. A newborn star whose dusty disc has been torn by a passing companion; when a streamer of that dust drifts across our line of sight the star fades for months. Watch its brightness, not its position.
target.kind: young star with a torn disc

colour.note: False colour: SPHEREx's infrared bands mapped to red, green and blue. Red means a source is brighter at longer wavelengths — cooler, dustier or more absorbed. Blue means the opposite. These are not visible-light colours.

stack.note: inverse-variance weighted mean of every exposure used

static.note: what stays put; subtract it mentally to see what moves

scale.note: one stretch shared by every frame so brightness is comparable

pixel_quality.note: Row-major npix*npix bitmask: bit i is set where any exposure flagged that pixel with class i. Used to explain why a pixel has no usable spectrum.

limits: SPHEREx pixels are 6.15 arcsec; close pairs blend together.
42 distinct bands measured here, out of 102 across the full survey. Each pixel sees one wavelength, set by its position on the filter.
Brightness is Level 2 surface brightness in MJy/sr, as delivered by IRSA. No photometry of our own.
Frames are bilinearly reprojected onto a common grid, which smooths noise slightly.
This is a display of public NASA data, not a detection claim.

classify.note: A point is 'odd one out' when its best template fits worse than 95% of randomly sampled points in this same field.

cube_u16.note: value = offset + code * scale per plane and frame; where the codec says transform 'log' (the variance plane) the value is exp() of that. Code 65535 means no data (flagged, non-finite, or zero variance) and must be skipped, exactly as the good mask is applied in Python
